title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Maker: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy remains distant.
why: This episode offers a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker of the real forms, costs, and AI boundaries of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it's directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers focused on modern warfare, the drone industry, and AI military applications.
skip: You can skip the opening company introduction and jump straight to the middle and later parts about AI and costs.

points.h: Producing nearly 100,000 a month, capacity still expanding
points.body: Founded in 2023, General Cherry initially produced only about 10 drones a month; now monthly output is around 100,000 (exact number undisclosed). The company works with over 110 military brigades, with the best units consuming more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still growing because battlefield consumption is enormous—drones have become expendables.

points.h: Hundreds of drone companies in Ukraine, but only 10–15 at the top
points.body: Ukraine may have up to 2,000 drone companies, but the vast majority are garage-style small workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet vast industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means intense competition.

points.h: AI models developed in-house, deep co-creation with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is fully self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and works closely with military units on the front lines. They gather battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This 'R&D–combat–feedback' loop lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt rapidly to the battlefield, rather than relying on external procurement.

points.h: Rocket-shaped FPV originated with Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; it was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sports events. Ukrainian companies discovered this shape could achieve higher speeds than standard quadcopters, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the fast-learning, pragmatic nature of Ukraine's drone industry—not seeking originality, only effectiveness.

points.h: A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
points.body: General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000 yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones worth $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is key to Ukraine's strategy against Russia's 'saturation attacks'—using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied costly air-defense missiles.

points.h: Interceptors confirmed to have downed over 5,000 Russian drones
points.body: General Cherry's tactical interceptor drones (General Trajectory Air) have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drone kills since production began in February 2025, with over 1,000 Russian 'Moniya' drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

points.h: AI runs on-device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. After an operator detects a target via radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This edge-AI design avoids battlefield communication delays and jamming, which is key to its practical viability.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying—killing would no longer require another human, only robots or drones. Currently they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to standard FPVs would significantly raise costs, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will drop, making future battlefields even more brutal.
